caseno: Appeal from Original Decree Nos. 121, 122 & 123 of 1960.
lawyer:
Md. Hafizullah, Nurul Islam ----- For the Appellant.
Khondker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Md. Shafiqur Rahman ----- for the Respondent.
parties:
Gladstone Wyllie & Co. Ltd ----- Appellant.
Vs.
A. B. M. Shayesta Khan and another ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
D.C. Bhattacharya, J.- These three appeals arise from three different Money Suits being money Suit No. 35 or 1955, Money Suit No. 31 of 1958 and Money Suit No. 9 of 1956. The first two or the Money Suits were brought by one A. B.M. Shayesta Khan against two Companies namely, Gladstone Wyllie and Co. Limited and Gladstone Lyall & Company Limited or recovery of lent and other reliefs in respect of a premises in the town of Chittagong. The other Money Suit was brought by the Gladstone Lyall & Company Limited, defendant No. 2 in the other two Money Suits, against the aforesaid A.R.M. Shayesta Khan for recovery of money by way of compensation for breach of contract. 

 2. The plaintiff's case in Money Suit No. 35 of 1955 and Money Suit No. 31 of 1958 in brief was that Gladstone Lyall & Company Limited, defendant No. 2 of he said two suits, advanced a sum of Tk. 72,000/- to the plaintiff for the construction of the said two Bungalows which were made for use and occupation of the said Company, they were made over to the possession of the said Company en 7-3-52 at the monthly rent of Tk. 950/- of which Tk. 600/- was to be set of against the total advance of Tk. 72.000/- and the remaining Tk. 350/- was to be paid in cash. According to the plaintiff, some frivolous and imaginary defects regarding one track road to the bungalows and the servants quarters were pointed out by the said Company in a letter dated 7-3-52 but the plaintiff wrote on 8-3-52 re pursuing the statements made ill the said letter uncut the same time authorising (he Company to make any constructions at their own costs and deduct the same against the rent of the premises. The plaintiff did not receive any further reference until the 26th June, 1953 when the said Company by a letter bearing the said date stated that they would suspend the payment of rent the track road to the Bungalows servant's quarters had not been completed. Plaintiff replied by his letter dated the 13th July, 1953 that he had already written to him on the 8th Match, 1952 authorising the Company to make necessary constructions and here again in this letter he was signifying his agreement to the said proposal of the Company made in their letter dated 7-3-52. It was the further case of the plaintiff that defendant No. 1 namely, Gladstone Wyllie & Compay Limited, was the successor of Gladstone Lyall and Company Limited and as such the former Company was liable for payment of the rent. 

 5: The claim in Money Suit No. 35 of 1955 was to recovery of rent for the period from March. 1952 to August, 1955. In the Money Suit No. 31 or 1958 the claim was laid in respect of the rent for the period from September, 1955 to August, 1958 and there was also a claim for damages in respect of the loss of certain materials. The allegations in the said two suits were more or less similar. 

 7. The learned Subordinate Judge, on a consideration or the cases of the parties and the evidence on record decreed Money Suit No. 35 of 1955 and 31 of 1958 in part and dismissed Money Suit No. 9 of 1956. The learned Sub-ordinate Judge in course of his judgment has come to the finding that the buildings including the track road and the servant quarters were constructed according to the specifications and that there was no breach of contract. He has further found that even it there were any defects in respect of the constructions they have been cured by the plaintiff’s acceptance of the proposal of Gladstone Lyall &. Company Limited, according to which tile said Company were to make the constructions at their own costs and adjust the rental of the premises. On the quest ion of the defence contention that Gladstone Wyllie & Company Limited is a company different from Gladstone Wyllie & Company Limited, the learned Subordinate Judge has held that they are one and the same Company and therefore Gladstone Wyllie & Company Limited cannot escape the liability of payment of rent in respect of the premises in suit. 

 8. On the basis of the said findings, both the suits were decreed against Gladstone Wyllie & Company Limited only. In Money Suit No. 31 of 1958 damages to the extent of Tk. 2,700/- on account of loss of both tubs and G.I. pipes for water connection and other articles was decreed in addition to the decree for arrear rent amounting to Tk. 12600/- . In Money Suit No. 35 of 1955 the learned Subordinate Judge took note of the fact that the two Bungalows had been requisitioned for a certain period, namely, one of the bungalow for one month and the other bungalow for 11 months. For the said period necessary remission was granted at the rate of Tk.175/- per month for each of the Bungalows. The learned Subordinate Judge has also found that in addition to Tk. 72,700/- paid in cash materials worth Tk. 6.960/- and odd were supplied and the cash rent of Tk. 350/- which was agreed to have been paid in the indenture was adjusted against the said Tk. 6,960/- and odd. 

 10. The appeals being F.A. Nos. 121 and 122 of 1960 have been preferred by Gladstone Wyllie & Company Limited against whom the decree in Money Suit No. 35 of 1955 and Money Suit No. 31 of 1958 have been passed and the appeal being F.A. No. 123 of 1960 has been preferred by Gladstone Lyall & Company Limited against the decree of dismissal of their suit being Money Suit No. 9 of 1956. 

 13. One of the main controversies which arises in these three suits is with regard to the nature of the agreement between the plaintiff Shayesta Khan and the other contracting party, Gladstone Lyall & Company Limited as to the kind of constructions which were to be made by the plaintiff and which were to constitute the subject-matter of the tenancy contemplated in the .Indenture Ext. 4(a) dated 17-11-50. The case of the plaintiff in Money Suit No. 35 of 1955 and 31 of 1958 is that he completed the constructions according to specifications and he made over possession of the same to the Company, Gladstone Lyall & Company Limited, The defence contention on the other hand, is that the plaintiff did not fulfill his part of the contract in regard to the said constructions  therefore is not entitled to enforce the Company's contractual obligation as to the payment of rent which according to the defendant was dependent upon the performance of the plaintiff's part of the contract. Some arguments have been made at the bar on the application of the doctrine of suspension of rent which cannot possibly be strictly applicable in the present case. The application of the said doctrine in its usual form is attracted in a case where the subject-matter of the tenancy has been made over to the possession of the tenant and the tenancy has commenced according to the term of the. agreement and if there after dispossession occurs at the instance of the landlord with regard to a part or whole of the holding of the tenancy, the tenant has a right to suspend the payment of the rent until possessor of the dispossessed part is restored to the tenant. The position in the instant case is certainly not analogous to the said circumstance. What is really contended by each Defendant Company is that payment of rent is one of the obligations which issue from the Indenture Ext. 4(a) and this payment or rent is dependent upon the making over possession of the bungalows according to the specifications made in the said deed for the use and occupation or the Company concerned. If it is really found that one of the contracting parties has failed to carry out his obligation under the contract of making the construction, and making over possession, of the house together with its adjuncts, for the use and occupation of the other contracting party, it is clear that the defaulting contracting party cannot unilaterally enforce the obligation of the other contracting party under the said contract, which is in the nature of a consequential obligation. The main question, therefore, which arises in this case is to see whether the plaintiff who wants to enforce the contractual obligation of payment of rent according to the Indenture Ext. 4(a) has really fulfilled his part of the obligation according to the said deed. Therefore, the first question which requires consideration in these appeals is whether the finding of the learned Subordinate Judge that there was no breach of contract as incorporated in Ext. 4(a) is consistent with the evidence on record. 

 39. So far as Money Suit No. 3 of 1958 is concerned the claim has been made for rent amounting to Tk. 12,600/- and damages for Tk. 11,759/8/6 pies for the loss of certain materials. The learned Subordinate Judge has given a decree for damages amounting to Tk. 2,700/- in addition to a decree for rent. These damages is with respect to the loss of bath tubs tor an amount of Tk. 700/-, G.I. pipes for an amount of Tk. 1000/- and other materials amounting to Tk. 1000/-. The evidence adduced by the plaintiff with regard to the loss of the materials has been given by the plaintiff himself and his son P.W.4. It has been admitted by P.W. 4 that no inventory of the articles was prepared at the time when possession was taken by the defendant Company. It is in the evidence of P.W. 2 that those electrical fittings and water pipes and electrical wires were damaged after the bungalows were derequisitioned and whatever damages occurred during the period of requisition have been repaired at the time when possession was given. This statement of the plaintiff is contradicted by his statement mace in his applicators Ext. G(2) dated 12-12-52 and Ext. G dated 10-3-54 in which the claim for compensation was made by the plaintiff to the District Magistrate for the damages caused to the buildings in the shape of removal of water tubs, electrical wiring and other damages amounting to Tk. 18,500/-. In this connection it may be mentioned that in Ext. 2(e) dated 7-3-52 it was stated by the defendant Company that bath rooms were not installed and it had been mentioned by the plaintiff himself in his alleged letter Ext. 2(v) that the defendant Company could fix up bath room at their own costs which would be deducted against the house-rent. The learned Subordinate Judge does not appear to have applied his mind to the evidence on record in regard to these tells of damages and has accepted the statement made by the plaintiff and his son without testing their veracity in the light of the other evidence on record. 

 43. One point still remains for decision as to whether Gladstone Wyllie & Company limited is the same as Gladstone Lyall & Company Limited. The learned Subordinate Judge has found that, the said two companies ate one and the same person and the basis ?f the findings is the lawyers letter Ext. 2(c) In which the notice giving lawyer on behalf of Gladstone Wyllie & Company Limited referred to the agreement Ext. 4 (a) and also to the letter dated 7-3-52, to which Gladstone Lyall & Company Limited was in fact the party, as the agreement and the letter to be by Gladstone Wyllie & Company Limited. In our opinion determination of this question will depend upon the actual legal character of the two companies and not upon an admission of a person. It is no doubt true that throughout the period Gladstone Wyllie & Company Limited were holding out themselves to be the representatives of Gladstone Lyall & Company Limited and were freely accepting the various actions done on behalf of Gladstone Lyall & Company Limited as their own. There is no doubt that Gladstone Wyllie & Company Limited was acting more or less as an agent or representative of Gladstone Lyall & Company Limited. to all intents and purposes, but the fact remains that the two are entirely different legal persons, one company being incorporated in Pakistan and the other company being incorporated in India. They cannot be regarded, in any event, as one and the same. In regard to the liability of rent of course, Gladstone Wyllie & Company and., was behaving as If they were the tenant and if the plaintiff had accepted them to be the tenant then of course there, would not have been any difficulty for the plaintiff to obtain a decree against them for rent, if any such decree could be passed at all. But the plaintiff had never accepted Gladstone Wyllie & Company limited as their tenant and all the house rent bills had been for warded to Gladstone Lyall & Company Limited. It is only Gladstone Lyall & Company Ltd. which has been described and recognised as the tenant in those bills, although in the Money Suits Gladstone Wyllie & Company Ltd. was representation Gladstone Lyall & Company Ltd. for all purposes. In the circumstances having regard to the facts that the plaintiff had never accepted Gladstone Wyllie & Company Limited as his tenant, no decree for rent can be passed against Gladstone Wyllie & Company Limited. If any decree can be passed In Money Suit No. 35 of 1955 or 31 of 1958 in respect of arrear rent, it can be passed only against Gladstone Lyall & Company Limited who was the tenant according to the deed of agreement Ext. 4(a). But in this case, as we have already held, the only amount which the plaintiff can claim by way of arrear rat is Tk. 9600/- in respect of certain period in Money Suit No. 35 of 1955 and as this amount has been allowed to be adjusted against the advance made by the Gladstone Lyall & Company Limited no decree can be passed in any of the two suits. 

 The result therefore is that all these three appeals are allowed with costs. Money Suit No. 35 of 1955 and Money Suit No. 31 of 1958, are dismissed with costs and Money Suit No. 9 of 1956 is decreed. in part with costs for an amount of Tk. 70,060/15/6 pies.
